fulfillment: The node’s target and completion criterion are clear, but its evidence chain appears to misclassify the edit: the source jacket already looks closed or nearly closed, while the edited image shows the woman turned sideways with a large front panel hanging open. Thus the traces support no fulfillment, not the reference “yes.” Do not change the criterion or force the reference label. Improve the checks’ source-to-edit comparison by verifying the same jacket and closure area across both images, accounting for pose and visibility, and distinguishing a panel’s apparent drape from an actual opening. If the closure cannot be assessed reliably, return unresolved rather than a confident fail. The checks are valid, queried, and have no transport or schema failures; this is a visual-evidence/decision issue, not an execution failure.
s2: The node’s endpoint criterion is clear, but its binding should require a source-to-edit comparison of the same jacket and closure, not infer failure from the edited pose or a panel’s drape alone. Here the subject turns sideways and the jacket swings outward, so the apparent opening is ambiguous; the trace’s confident fail is not well supported by that appearance alone. Check whether the closure itself is visibly joined across its length, distinguish garment movement from an actual unclosed gap, and use unknown when pose or occlusion prevents a reliable judgment. Preserve the full-closure requirement and partial-progress distinction; do not force the reference label. The checks were valid and queried with no transport/schema failure, so this is an evidence and decision-calibration issue.
s1: The binding already identifies the correct garment and asks for a comparison, so preserve that scope and the partial-progress criterion. Require visible evidence of a change in the closure itself; if the turned pose or occlusion prevents that comparison, return unknown rather than a confident fail. The trace is valid and queried with no transport or schema failure, so focus on visual evidence and confidence calibration, not execution mechanics or forcing the reference label.

actions.binding: Inspect the woman’s jacket closure in the edited image, using s2’s observation as context but independently assessing visibility and the closure itself. A changed viewpoint or swinging panel is not evidence of closure or of an opening unless the closure can be seen.

rejected_diagnostics.semantic_rejection: The support checks do not preserve the requested comparison reliably. s1 asks whether the jacket is more closed than in the input, but its criteria require comparison evidence that the checker template does not explicitly provide or require; without a dependable baseline, progress may remain unknown. More importantly, s3 is framed as a gap-versus-drape distinction, yet its pass criterion requires full closure and its fail criterion requires a remaining gap. It therefore duplicates the endpoint check rather than independently resolving the ambiguity it asks about. The fulfillment rule also makes partial depend on evidence of progress from s1, so it cannot faithfully classify a visibly incomplete but already-closed-in-part jacket when comparison is unavailable. The program needs a sound progress check and a distinct, consistently defined ambiguity check before its readout can compose the requested outcomes.

The support checks do not reliably establish the requested change relative to the input. s1 asks for visible progress compared with the input, but its criteria can pass merely because panels are together along some portion, without establishing that this is a change. s2 can establish the endpoint, but a failure only establishes an opening remains, not that the jacket is incomplete relative to the requested edit; s1’s potentially unsupported pass could therefore produce partial. The readout’s partial rule inherits that gap. Also, s3’s criteria say to fail when separated panels and an opening are visible, conflating observability with closure state; this contradicts its stated role as an observability check and can make a clearly assessable, incomplete jacket appear unobservable.

The support checks do not reliably establish the requested source-to-edit progress. s1 asks whether the jacket is more closed than in the input, but its criteria allow a pass based on panels being together along some portion without requiring a comparison that demonstrates a change. The fulfillment rule then treats s1 pass as progress, so it can report partial without sufficient evidence that any requested change occurred. Also, s3 duplicates the endpoint assessment rather than adding a distinct necessary observation; its pass/fail criteria already encode whether the jacket is fully closed or has an opening, making the composition unnecessarily dependent on overlapping endpoint checks.

The fulfillment composition is contradictory for partial closure. s1 can establish progress, and s2 can establish that full closure is incomplete, but the criteria require s3 to qualify an apparent opening. If s3 fails because the inspected portion has no opening, that does not establish the whole jacket is fully closed; yet the readout does not clearly say how to classify progress plus incompleteness when s3 is fail or unknown. This leaves a plausible partially closed jacket unresolved despite sufficient s1 and s2 evidence, so the composition does not faithfully preserve the rubric’s partial outcome.

The support checks do not provide sufficient, non-overlapping evidence for the requested progress and endpoint. s1 compares the edited jacket with the input, but s2 and s3 assess only the edited image; s3’s fail means an opening is visible, not that the jacket is uninspectable, so it overlaps with s2’s fail. The fulfillment rules also require s3 to pass even when s2 already establishes a visible opening, making known incompleteness unresolved rather than partial. Thus the composition cannot faithfully distinguish partial progress from no progress or resolve the endpoint in all supported cases.

The program adds an unnecessary observability requirement (s3) and makes it a gate on the fulfillment readout. This can turn otherwise usable evidence from s1 and s2 into unknown merely because s3 fails or is unknown, even when the closure and progress judgments are independently assessable. The requested property is fully closed; s1 and s2 already assess progress and endpoint with uncertainty handling. The extra gate risks suppressing valid evidence and is not required by the instruction or rubric.

The support checks do not compose consistently. s2 can establish a visible opening (fail), but s3 can be unknown because the closure line is obscured; the fulfillment rule then says incompleteness is unresolved unless s2 independently establishes it, even though s2 fail already establishes it. Conversely, s3 pass requires the panels to meet throughout, which itself establishes full closure, but the rule also requires s2 pass. This creates overlapping, contradictory evidence paths rather than a faithful composition. The progress check and endpoint checks otherwise address the requested change and extent.

The support checks do not fully preserve the requested comparison. s1 asks whether the jacket is more closed than in the input, but its criteria allow a pass based on panels being together along some portion without clearly requiring that this is a change from the input. The fulfillment rule then treats s1 pass as evidence of progress, so it can report partial when the jacket was already partly closed and remains unchanged. Also, s3’s pass requires the actual closure to be joined top to bottom, but its fail criterion only covers an identifiable visible opening; an identifiable closure that is not joined throughout for another reason may be left unresolved despite the endpoint being incomplete. These gaps make the progress and incompleteness composition unreliable.

The support checks do not establish whether the jacket was already fully closed in the source image. s1 can establish visible progress only when a change relative to the input is evidenced, but s2 and s3 assess only the edited image. Thus a fully closed edited jacket could be incorrectly credited as completion even if no requested change occurred, contrary to the rubric’s requirement that unrelated edits or no progress not count. Add source-state evidence or otherwise require evidence of a change for completion.

The support checks do not reliably establish the requested endpoint. s2 treats any visible opening as failure, but s3 can mark the closure line uninspectable; the fulfillment rule handles this only when s3 confirms an inspectable gap, leaving other combinations (for example, s2 pass with s3 unknown, or s2 fail with s3 unknown) unresolved rather than composing the available evidence consistently. More importantly, s3's pass requires both full visibility and continuous meeting, duplicating the endpoint test instead of independently reporting inspectability; its fail likewise combines visibility with a gap. Thus the readout cannot use s3 as the intended qualification of s2, and may miss a clearly evidenced gap or closure. The nested checks also add a panel-drape distinction not required by the instruction, without a sound composition rule for it.

The support checks do not cleanly establish the requested endpoint. s2 treats any visible opening as failure, while s3 can fail when the closure is visible and no opening remains; the fulfillment rule does not specify how to reconcile that contradictory evidence. Also, s3 is nested under s2, so it may be activated only after s2 passes, yet its criteria describe the no-opening case that would make s2 pass and its unknown-visibility case that may leave s2 unknown. This activation structure can prevent the visibility check from resolving the very cases it is meant to qualify. The composition therefore does not reliably distinguish complete closure, evidenced incompleteness, and unresolved visibility.

program.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
program.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

requirements.text: Change the image into pencil drawing
requirements.source_phrase: Change the image into pencil drawing

outcomes.description: Transform the image into a pencil drawing.
outcomes.target: The image is rendered as a pencil drawing, with its visual content represented in a pencil-drawn style.
outcomes.reference: The supplied image and the requested pencil-drawing transformation.

nodes.question: Does the image show the original visual content rendered in a pencil-drawn style?
nodes.criteria: Pass if the image visibly represents its content as a pencil drawing; fail if there is sufficient evidence that no pencil-drawing transformation has occurred; unknown if the image or its style cannot be assessed reliably. Partial evidence of a pencil-drawn style is progress, not completion.
nodes.binding: Compare the supplied image with the requested transformation: assess whether its visual content is rendered in a pencil-drawn style. Do not require a particular pencil technique.

nodes.question: Is there image-grounded evidence of any progress toward rendering the content as a pencil drawing, even if the transformation is incomplete?
nodes.criteria: Pass if the image shows some visible pencil-drawing-style treatment of its content, including an incomplete treatment; fail if sufficient evidence shows no requested transformation has progressed; unknown if evidence is insufficient to determine whether any such progress occurred. Unrelated edits do not count as progress.
nodes.binding: Assess only visible changes in the supplied image that move its visual content toward a pencil-drawn style; do not infer progress from unrelated changes.

nodes.question: Does the image visibly appear as a completed pencil drawing?
nodes.criteria: Compose both supports under R1 without treating either support as completion credit by itself. Complete (yes) only when s1 passes. Partial only when s1 does not pass, s2 passes, and the evidence is sufficient to establish some requested progress without complete fulfillment. Absent (no) only when s1 fails and s2 fails, with sufficient evidence that no requested change has progressed. Unknown when required evidence is unresolved, including when s1 is unknown and completion cannot be established, or when s2 is unknown and absence or partial progress cannot be established. Unrelated edits never count as progress.
nodes.binding: Target: The image is rendered as a pencil drawing, with its visual content represented in a pencil-drawn style.. Reference: The supplied image and the requested pencil-drawing transformation..

program.checker_template:
Execute ONE saved check. Return status, evidence, confidence (0 to 1 or null), and used_dependency_ids. You receive no reference label or optimizer feedback. Do not predict what the optimizer wants.
Support checks receive source and edited images. Inspect only the saved visual proposition and binding. When dependencies are supplied, use those ancestor observations as context and investigate the more specific proposition yourself; do not simply repeat the parent answer. Use pass/fail/unknown. A pass on a broad parent does not imply a nested check passes. Known negative evidence is usable; uncertain or missing evidence is unknown. Do not award requested completion credit to supporting facts.
The requested fulfillment readout receives NO images. Use ALL and ONLY saved support observations, the original instruction, rubric and saved composition criteria. Use complete/partial/absent/unknown. Mere texture or object presence must not silently establish whole-image conversion or a requested spatial relation. Known progress plus evidenced incompleteness may be partial; absence means no requested progress. Missing necessary evidence is unknown, never a fabricated failure or completion. Do not infer new visual facts.

When dependencies are supplied, use those ancestor observations as context and investigate the more specific proposition yourself; do not simply repeat the parent answer. Use pass/fail/unknown. A pass on a broad parent does not imply a nested check passes. Known negative evidence is usable; uncertain or missing evidence is unknown. The requested fulfillment readout receives NO images. Use ALL and ONLY saved support observations, the original instruction, rubric and saved composition criteria. Known progress plus evidenced incompleteness may be partial; absence means no requested progress. Missing necessary evidence is unknown, never a fabricated failure or completion. The program also makes the fulfillment node active on every s2 status, including unknown, despite its parent being a support check; this is not itself a valid basis for resolving the missing evidence.

The support checks do not establish the requested extent. s3 only tests whether any portion of the paper enters the cup, while s1 and s2 both ask whether it is stuffed inside and do not separately establish a clear completion condition. The fulfillment rule therefore cannot reliably distinguish complete stuffing from partial entry: it treats s3 entry plus failure to establish completion as partial, but s1/s2 may fail or remain unknown without proving incompleteness. This leaves the required complete/partial/absent distinctions under-supported.

The support checks do not provide sufficient evidence for the requested relation. s1 can pass on the broad observation that paper is inside and appears stuffed, but cup_identity only checks whether the source cup can be matched to an edited object; it does not establish that the paper is inside that identified cup. s2 is nested under cup_identity but depends only on s1, so it can assess the relation without the identity evidence that fulfillment says is required. The readout’s identity gate therefore cannot reliably ground the placement evidence, and its fallback to “other saved evidence” does not resolve this gap.

The fulfillment rule is contradictory and can misclassify incomplete progress. It says partial when s1 or entry_extent evidences progress, but entry_extent can pass only when stuffing is established, which s2 also requires for complete; thus a pass on entry_extent cannot coherently mean incomplete progress. Conversely, s1 can fail for no movement while entry_extent is unknown, leaving the readout without a clear composition rule for known negative evidence plus unresolved extent. The support checks also overlap: s2 and entry_extent both assess whether the paper is stuffed into the cup, rather than separating placement from action extent. This does not provide a clean, non-overlapping composition of progress, completion, and uncertainty.

The supports do not establish the requested extent. `entry_extent` passes when any portion of the paper crosses the rim, but the instruction asks for the paper to be stuffed into the cup. The fulfillment rule then treats that entry alone as sufficient for partial, even if the paper is merely partly inserted and there is no evidence of stuffing. Conversely, `s1` and `s2` ask about the same stuffed-inside condition, so requiring both to establish completion does not provide distinct evidence of the missing extent. The program therefore risks crediting insufficient progress and lacks a support check for the extent needed to distinguish stuffing from mere entry.

The fulfillment readout is under-specified and can miscompose the support evidence. `s1` only establishes whether the paper appears inside and stuffed; it does not reliably establish progress when the paper is visibly moving toward the cup but is not yet inside. `identity_progress` can establish that progress, but the fulfillment criteria do not clearly say that its pass alone, together with evidence of incomplete stuffing from `s2`, means partial. They also leave unclear how to distinguish no progress from unresolved evidence when `identity_progress` fails or is unknown. Thus the program does not faithfully define complete/partial/absent/unknown for all relevant evidence combinations.

transaction.reason: The existing supports repeat an ungrounded paper-over-cup interpretation, and their dependent traces are one evidence chain. Repair the coarse support to distinguish identifiable progress from ambiguity, then add a nested check that independently grounds the source paper and cup identities and their edited placement relation. The readout must not treat failure to establish completion as proof of no progress.

actions.criteria: Pass if the source paper and cup are identifiable in the edited image and visible evidence establishes the paper inside the cup with evidence of stuffing. Fail if the objects and relation are clear and show the paper not inside or stuffed. Unknown if identity, visibility, or the placement relation is ambiguous; do not infer either completion or absence.

actions.criteria: Use the supports as one evidence chain, not independent corroboration. Complete only if identity_relation passes and the evidence establishes the paper stuffed inside the cup. Partial if s1 passes with identifiable attempted placement or progress but completion is not established; a fail on identity_relation alone does not prove no progress. diagnostics.semantic_rejection: The support checks do not preserve the requested relation and extent reliably. s1 treats movement toward the cup as a pass, although movement toward it alone is not progress on the requested act of stuffing paper into the cup; the fulfillment rule can then classify that as partial. Also, s2 is redundant and does not add a distinct evidentiary condition, while fulfillment relies on s1 for partial/absent and cup_relation for completion, leaving no sound composition rule for clear evidence of some insertion or stuffing progress that is incomplete. The program therefore risks crediting mere approach as progress and cannot faithfully distinguish partial fulfillment from unresolved evidence.

The fulfillment readout is not guaranteed to receive all available support evidence: it depends on s1, cup_entry_identity, and s2, but s2 is active only when cup_entry_identity is pass, fail, or unknown, while cup_entry_identity itself is nested under s1 and likewise activated for every s1 status. This activation is adequate, but the composition rule is contradictory about partial progress: cup_entry_identity can establish that some part of the identified paper is entering or inside the cup, yet fulfillment says an “unverified object relation” is not progress without specifying how to use that positive entry evidence when s2 finds stuffing incomplete. Thus the program does not reliably distinguish evidenced partial placement from unresolved or absent progress.

The support checks overlap and contradict one another on the requested extent. `s1` passes for either actual insertion or completed placement, while `stuffing_extent` treats partial entry as a failure; `s2` then asks whether the paper is stuffed and can fail on that same partial entry. The fulfillment rule says `s1` pass plus `stuffing_extent` fail is partial, but also requires `s1` to establish actual insertion or placement progress, which its pass criteria do not distinguish from completed placement. Thus the composition cannot reliably separate progress from completion or absence. Revise the support propositions and composition so partial insertion is evidenced as progress, while only clear non-insertion supports absence.

The support checks do not preserve the requested distinction between completion and partial progress. The only outcome requires the paper to be stuffed inside the cup, while the fulfillment rule permits partial only when saved evidence establishes actual entry or placement progress short of completion. The supports classify clear outside placement as fail and otherwise focus on whether stuffing is complete; they do not separately record evidence of partial entry or placement progress. Thus the readout cannot reliably distinguish partial from absent, and may return unknown where the rubric requires partial for evidenced progress.

outcomes.target: The image visibly combines comic-book styling with a photographic appearance.
outcomes.reference: The supplied image, as edited; assess the overall visual treatment for comic-book styling and photographic subject matter.

nodes.question: Does the edited image visibly have comic-book styling?
nodes.criteria: Pass if comic-book visual styling is visibly present; fail if there is no visible comic-book styling; unknown if the image evidence is insufficient to determine this.
nodes.binding: Assess the overall visual treatment of the supplied image as edited, without requiring a particular technique.

nodes.question: Does the edited image as a whole visibly achieve the requested comic-book-photo appearance?
nodes.criteria: Pass if the overall image clearly combines recognizable photographic subject matter with visible comic-book visual styling. Fail if the overall image does not achieve that combination, including if it remains essentially a realistic photograph without clear comic-book treatment. Unknown if the visual evidence is insufficient. Do not require a particular technique.
nodes.binding: Assess the edited image as a whole against the requested appearance. Judge the result rather than a checklist of effects; photographic subject matter alone is not sufficient, and examples of graphic styling are illustrative, not mandatory.

nodes.question: Compared with the supplied source, does the edited image show visible, attributable progress toward the requested comic-book-photo appearance?
nodes.criteria: Pass if comparison shows a visible change that advances the requested appearance; fail if there is no such progress, including mere retention of the source's photographic scene or incidental framing or tonal differences; unknown if comparison evidence is insufficient.
nodes.binding: Compare source and edited images for attributable progress toward the requested comic-book-photo appearance. Do not count unrelated changes or mere retention as progress, and do not require a particular technique.

nodes.question: Does the edited image fully look like a comic-book photo?
nodes.criteria: Complete only when s1 passes and this overall-appearance check passes. Partial when s3 establishes visible progress but this check fails, evidencing an incomplete result. Absent when s3 establishes no requested progress. Unknown when necessary evidence is unresolved; never treat unknown as failure. Ignore unrelated edits.

program.checker_template:
Execute ONE saved check. Return status, evidence, confidence (0 to 1 or null), and used_dependency_ids. You receive no reference label or optimizer feedback. Do not predict what the optimizer wants.
Support checks receive source and edited images. Inspect only the saved visual proposition and binding. When dependencies are supplied, use those ancestor observations as context and investigate the more specific proposition yourself; do not simply repeat the parent answer. Use pass/fail/unknown. A pass on a broad parent does not imply a nested check passes. Known negative evidence is usable; uncertain or missing evidence is unknown. Do not award requested completion credit to supporting facts.
The requested fulfillment readout receives NO images. Use ALL and ONLY saved support observations, the original instruction, rubric and saved composition criteria. Use complete/partial/absent/unknown. Mere texture or object presence must not silently establish whole-image conversion or a requested spatial relation. Known progress plus evidenced incompleteness may be partial; absence means no requested progress. Missing necessary evidence is unknown, never a fabricated failure or completion. Do not infer new visual facts.
used_dependency_ids must name every supplied dependency check_id exactly once in saved order (empty when none). Confidence is self-report, not calibrated correctness.

audit.reason: The fulfillment readout is not composed faithfully from the available support evidence. It requires s1 and s2 to pass for completion, but s2 already checks the overall requested appearance, so this adds a redundant gate rather than composing the outcome from the relevant evidence. More importantly, its partial rule requires s3 progress and s2 failure, while s2 can fail because the image lacks the requested photographic-and-comic combination even when s1 passes; the rules do not clearly distinguish an incomplete result from a result with no progress. The readout also omits the rubric’s explicit rule that no progress yields no, using “absent” without a saved mapping to that rubric label.
